title: The resurrection of the body
hookLine: not escape from the body, but bodies raised and made new

lines: A SOUL ON A CLOUD, WITH A HARP?
cards: Ask most people what Christians think happens after death, and you'll hear this: your soul floats out of your body to heaven, where it lives forever on a cloud, maybe with a harp. The body stays behind, like an old coat.
Read the creed carefully, and it says something stranger, and more solid. Near the very end, just before life everlasting: I believe in the resurrection of the body. Not the escape of the soul.
The body. Raised. Your hands, your face, your voice, somehow, made new.

teach.h: NOT A PRISON FOR THE SOUL.
teach.b: In the ancient world, plenty of thinkers taught that the body was a prison for the soul, and death was a release. Early Christians knew those ideas, and turned them down. Their hope was built on Easter.
The risen Jesus wasn't a ghost.
In Luke, he says: touch me and see, a spirit doesn't have flesh and bones. He eats a piece of fish in front of them. In John, he still carries the marks of the nails.
And yet he's changed: he appears in locked rooms, and friends don't recognize him at first.

teach.h: A SEED, AND WHAT GROWS FROM IT.
teach.b: Christians say what happened to Jesus is a first taste of what will happen to everyone. Paul's picture is a seed. You plant a bare seed, and up comes a whole plant, connected to the seed but far more glorious.
"It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption." "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." A spiritual body isn't made of air.
It's a body fully alive with God's Spirit, no longer dying. Paul admits there's a great deal we don't know about what that will be like.

teach.h: ALL THINGS NEW, SO BODIES MATTER NOW.
teach.b: The Bible's last book pictures not souls leaving the earth, but a new heaven and a new earth, and God saying: "Behold, I make all things new."

teach.h: IT IS SOWN IN CORRUPTION; IT IS RAISED IN INCORRUPTION.
teach.b: That's why Christians have cared so much for bodies: burying the dead with honor, running hospitals, feeding the hungry. Many churches now allow cremation too; the hope doesn't depend on what happens to the remains.
If God will raise bodies, then bodies matter now: yours, and everyone else's.

how: Christians say "the resurrection of the body" in the Apostles' Creed, and at funerals many churches pray in the hope of the resurrection, burying or committing the body with honor.

games.q: the disciples are terrified. they think they're seeing a ghost. you're the risen Jesus. what do you do?
o: vanish, and speak from the air.
tell them to touch you, and eat a piece of fish.
tell them the body doesn't matter anymore.
games.why: in Luke, Jesus says to touch him and see, since a spirit hasn't flesh and bones, and he eats in front of them.

practice: Picture your body as Paul pictured it: a seed, not a shell you'll shed, with more in it than it looks, even the parts worn or scarred or aching, which Christians say are not thrown away.
Then hold in mind, for a few breaths, someone else's body you love that is tired or ill or old.
If you pray, give thanks to God for your body and theirs, and for the hope that both will be raised; if you don't, simply be grateful for them.

wordCard.voice: Soma. Paul's Greek word for body, used even for the spiritual body raised at the resurrection: not escaped, but made new.

orig.note: Greek: body. Paul's soma pneumatikon, spiritual body, is still a body.

carryVoice: Your line: bodies matter. A seed, not a shell, and made new. That's three hundred ten.
